instruction: Judge whether the rewrite preserves all substantive reasoning of the original, without omissions, unsupported additions or changes in actor, mechanism, condition, timing, scope, direction or effect. Use preserved only if all survive, changed for a material difference, uncertain if unresolved. Give specific evidence. Independently map each supplied original source passage index to the closest corresponding exact contiguous quotation in the rewrite; use null if absent. A quote can identify a changed relation; it is not a vote that the relation was preserved. Quotes are for analysis only.

documents.original:
The breeze at the gate can feel quite different from the breeze out on the grass. A windsock near the middle lets people pick a launch direction before they unroll a line. Everyone tends to launch from the same bare patch. Moving the launch flags a little each week gives the grass time to grow back. Peg a bright ribbon to the top of each low fence post along the ditch so flyers looking up can still catch sight of the boundary.

Children like to watch from directly under the kites. A bench with a good view off to one side gives families a comfortable spot clear of the lines. A kite in the big oak is tempting to climb after. Put the groundskeeper's contact details on the tree guard so the owner can arrange to get it back from ground level. A child who drops a backpack at the edge of the field can lose sight of it when other families arrive. Hooks along the inside of the gate give bags a place that's easy to find again.
documents.rewrite:
Set a windsock well out on the grass, near the middle of the field. The wind there can differ from what you feel at the gate, and flyers can look at the sock to choose a direction before unwinding their lines. Shift the launch flags a short distance each week. People tend to use one patch until it's bare, and moving the flags gives it a chance to recover. Fasten a bright ribbon to the top of every low fence post beside the ditch so that even someone watching a kite overhead can glimpse the field boundary.

Give families a bench to one side with a clear view of the kites. Children can watch comfortably there, away from the lines, instead of gathering right underneath. On the guard around the big oak, post a way to reach the groundskeeper. Anyone whose kite gets caught can stay on the ground and arrange to get it back without climbing the tree. Fit bag hooks just inside the gate, too. Children can find a backpack there even after more families arrive and the edge of the field fills up.

A quartet can set up much faster if it knows what is already in the room. Put a dated equipment list beside the booking form so players can decide what to bring. A cello endpin slides on the polished floor. Keep a few endpin stops with the chairs so cellists can play without chasing their instruments forward. Put a pencil groove or clip on each music stand. Players mark bowings as they rehearse, and a pencil that stays on the stand is always within reach.

Store spare scores upright in folders labeled by ensemble. Loose sheets from different arrangements otherwise end up together, taking time to sort before the first piece. A clock visible from the conductor's spot makes it easier to leave time for the last piece without breaking off to check a phone. Ask visitors before recording a rehearsal. Someone who is uncomfortable being recorded then has time to speak up before a take begins.
documents.rewrite:
Keep an equipment list next to the booking form and put a date on it. A quartet can see what to pack before arriving and spend less of its rehearsal setting up. Store a few endpin stops alongside the chairs so the cellos stay put on the polished floor. Fit every stand with a clip or groove for a pencil, ready to hand when a player wants to mark a bowing.

File spare scores vertically in folders bearing the ensembles' names. That saves players from having to separate loose pages from different arrangements before they can start the first piece. Hang a clock where the conductor can read it while conducting and allow enough time for the final piece without stopping to look at a phone. If you'd like to record a rehearsal, ask the visitors first so anyone uneasy about it has a chance to say so before the take starts.

Ask residents to mark a small box on the signup slip if they prefer a doorstep copy. People who rarely get to the shops would still receive the bulletin. Lists of events go stale quickly on a crowded counter. Give the issue date a prominent place on the front so readers can pick out this week's edition. Stairs make a crate of several hundred copies awkward to handle. Split it into smaller bundles at the print shop so volunteers can carry one manageable load at a time.

Paper carriers sometimes fall ill on delivery morning. Pair each route with a backup who already knows the stops so that week's issue still goes out. Pick a consistent day for replenishing the racks. Readers who make just one shopping trip a week can then plan to collect a fresh copy. A full rack by the checkout is easy to overlook among the sale leaflets. A small sign above it telling shoppers the bulletin is free gives them a reason to take one.
documents.rewrite:
Give residents a small box to tick on the signup slip for delivery to their door. That way, people who seldom visit the shops can still get the paper. Put the issue date where it stands out on the front. On a counter crowded with notices, readers can spot this week's events before they pick up an old edition. At the print shop, break each crate of several hundred copies into bundles a volunteer can comfortably carry up the stairs one at a time.

Arrange for a second person who knows the stops on each route to cover if the regular carrier wakes up ill on delivery day. The neighborhood can still get that week's paper. Restock the racks on the same day every week so people who shop only once a week can time their trip for a fresh issue. Hang a small sign above the checkout rack saying the bulletin is free. Even when the rack is full, it's easy for shoppers to miss it among the sale flyers, and the sign invites them to take a copy.

Try the lamp before the families arrive. A cool-running LED that casts one clean shadow lets children handle the figures nearby and keeps the outlines easy to follow. Make a few large loop handles for children who find a narrow stick difficult to hold. They can move their own characters without an adult taking over. Let children try moving the same puppet toward and away from the lamp. Seeing its shadow grow and shrink gives them a way to turn a small character into a giant.

Leave a clear approach to one side of the screen at seated height. A child using a wheelchair can bring a puppet into the same scene as a standing partner. Put a piece of scrap card under each figure when punching holes for joints. The hole comes out clean and the hall tables stay free of dents. Children behind the sheet can't see the faces out front. Let pairs trade places after each short scene so they can see how their work looks from the audience.
documents.rewrite:
Before the families come in, test a cool-running LED and check that each puppet makes a single, distinct shadow. Children can work close to the light and the audience can follow the outlines. Give children who struggle to grip the thin sticks the option of a large loop handle. They can then move their own characters without handing them to an adult. Invite them to take one puppet closer to the lamp and then farther away. They can watch it grow and shrink on the screen and use that effect to make a little character into a giant.

Keep one side of the screen clear all the way up to a spot a child can reach while seated. A wheelchair user and a standing partner can bring their puppets into the same scene there. Slip scrap card beneath each figure before punching its joint holes to get a neat hole and spare the hall tables any dents. Children working behind the sheet miss the faces of the people watching. Have partners swap sides after every short scene so each gets to see the performance from the audience.

A row of card stacks hides most of the pictures. Prop up one of each design so visitors can pick out a view they recognize. Postage depends on where the card is going, so have the stamp volunteer ask the destination before handing over a stamp. That keeps a card for overseas from leaving with domestic postage. A child may have a whole story to send before they can form the letters. A volunteer who takes dictation can get the child's own words onto the card.

Print the town and today's date on a small sign at the writing places. Visitors who want to mark the occasion can copy both without interrupting a conversation. A gust can carry half a dozen postcards across the square. Tuck the outdoor stock under a broad paperweight so people can lift out one card at a time. Test the pens on an actual postcard before opening. A pen that skips on the glossy stock can be replaced before it spoils someone's message.
documents.rewrite:
Stand one sample of each postcard upright. The other designs can be hard to see when the stacks are lined up, and a display lets visitors choose a familiar view. Ask the volunteer handling stamps to find out where each card is headed before giving out postage. The destination determines the stamp, and an overseas card could otherwise go out with only domestic postage. If a child has a story to tell but can't yet write the letters, offer to write down exactly what they say.

Set a small printed sign with the town's name and today's date beside the writing spots. People who want a record of the occasion can copy the details while conversations carry on. Outdoors, hold the supply down with a wide paperweight. Visitors can slide out one card while the rest stay put if a gust blows across the square. Before you open, try the pens on a postcard from the table and replace any that skip on its glossy surface, before someone starts a message with one.

A volunteer collecting a large wedding order may arrive on foot. Include the number of packed crates in the pickup note so they can arrange a ride if needed. Crumbs and a forgotten dessert fork can disappear inside a folded cloth. Ask the clearing crew to shake each one over a bin before bagging it so the washer gets fabric alone. Rough crate edges can catch embroidery. Line the crates with smooth covers so moving a loan between buildings doesn't pull threads loose.

Put an aisle and shelf number on each return bin. A new volunteer can then put clean linen away where the next order will be picked. When a group's tables have different shapes, pack by room and table number. Its setup crew can take each bundle straight to the right spot. Send a return receipt after the hall checks in the loan. The group can close its event file knowing whether it still needs to search for a missing piece.
documents.rewrite:
Tell the person collecting a loan how many packed crates to expect in the pickup note. Someone planning to walk over for a large wedding order will have time to arrange a lift if they need one. For groups using differently shaped tables, sort the linen into bundles by room and table number so the people setting up can deliver each bundle to its table. Use smooth liners in the crates. A rough edge can snag embroidery and pull out threads during the trip from one building to another.

Have the people clearing tables shake out every cloth over a bin before it goes in the bag. Crumbs and even a dessert fork can hide in the folds, and only linen should reach the washer. Mark each return bin with both the aisle and shelf where the clean pieces belong. Even a first-time volunteer can put them where the next person filling an order will look. Once the hall has checked the loan back in, send the group a receipt. It can close the event file knowing whether there is still a piece to track down.

Walk the route at the planned hour a few days ahead. A fountain or a delivery truck that runs every morning might otherwise drown out the first stop. At a corner where birds often answer each other, pause for a second phrase. It can reveal that the sound from the hedge is coming from two directions. Pass around a simple outline map and let people mark where they heard a song. They can return to that corner on a later walk and listen again.

Keep ringtones off during listening stops. An electronic chirp from a pocket can sound remarkably like another bird joining in. A busy road crossing needs everyone's attention. Finish the listening stop before the curb so the group can concentrate on getting across together. Leave time at the finish for each walker to share one sound they want to recognize again. The guide can match each description to a recording or field-guide entry they can revisit.
documents.rewrite:
A few days before the walk, follow the route at the hour you've chosen for the event. You'll hear whether a fountain or a regular morning delivery would mask the birds at the first stop. Where birds often call back and forth, pause at that corner for a second phrase before moving on. People may then hear that the calls in the hedge come from two directions. Pass a simple outline map around so walkers can mark where they heard a song and find the corner again on another outing.

Ask everyone to silence their ringtones at listening stops, since a chirp from someone's pocket can easily sound like a new bird joining in. Near a busy crossing, wrap up the listening before reaching the curb so everyone can give their attention to crossing together. Save a few minutes at the end for each person to describe one sound they'd like to know next time. The guide can point each walker to a matching recording or field-guide entry to return to later.

Someone choosing a pen for a daily planner needs to know how it behaves on those pages. Leave room for them to try a few words in their own planner as well. Arrange the pens in shallow grooved trays. A visitor can set one down to inspect the writing without having it roll onto the floor. A fountain pen can make a line under its own weight. Demonstrate that on a scrap before handing it over so a newcomer can start without bearing down on the nib.

A cap left off while people talk can leave the next visitor with a dry nib. Give the person finishing a turn the job of recapping the pen. A couple of ordinary loops can feel comfortable even with a pen that's tiring over time. Offer enough space to write a full paragraph and judge the grip. Show which pens the owners are happy to have used with the cap on the back. Visitors can explore how the extra weight feels without guessing what a borrowed pen will tolerate.
documents.rewrite:
Give visitors space to bring out their own daily planner and write a few words in it if that's where they intend to use a pen. They can see how it writes on the actual pages. Set the pens out in shallow trays with grooves. When someone puts a pen down to look over their writing, it will stay in place without rolling off onto the floor. Before passing a fountain pen to a beginner, use a scrap of paper to show how it draws a line with just its own weight. They'll know how lightly they can touch the nib to the page.

Make recapping the pen part of finishing a turn. If people start chatting with the cap off, the nib may be dry by the time someone else picks it up. Give each visitor room for a whole paragraph, since a grip that feels fine for a couple of loops can tire the hand with longer use. Indicate which owners are happy for visitors to fit the cap onto the back of their pen as they write. People can feel how that weight changes the pen without having to guess whether it's OK to try it on a borrowed one.
